pairs.rationale: Both acknowledge inevitable stumbling blocks while pronouncing woe on their human source. Matthew additionally says woe to the world; Luke directly addresses disciples.
Both prefer a millstone and drowning to causing a little one to stumble. Matthew specifies little ones believing in Jesus; Luke does not repeat that qualification here.
Both direct confronting a brother's sin. Matthew specifies private correction and gaining a brother who listens; Luke explicitly links repentance with forgiveness.
Both address repeated forgiveness using seven. Luke specifies seven offenses and repentant returns within a day; Matthew records Peter's question and Jesus' greater numerical answer.
Both appeals ask Jesus for help with deficient faith. Luke's apostles request increased faith; Mark's father confesses belief and asks help for unbelief. The speakers and circumstances differ.
Both use mustard-seed faith and an apparently impossible command. Luke pictures uprooting a mulberry tree into the sea; Matthew pictures moving a mountain.
Luke17 questions immediately seating a working slave at the master's table; Luke12 promises the exceptional master serving watchful slaves. The contrasting service arrangements are preserved.
Both mention girding and meal service, with reversed roles. Here the slave serves before eating; there the returning master girds himself and serves the watchful slaves.

The question about thanking a slave for commanded work leads to the same episode's application: servants have only done their duty. The application is not independent attestation of a household custom.
Both distinguish required service from a claim to credit. Luke's slaves have done what they ought; Paul has no boast in proclaiming because necessity lies upon him. Their commissions differ.
Both locate Jesus' movement toward Jerusalem. Luke17 specifies passage through Samaria and Galilee; Luke9 introduces His resolve and approaching taking-up, without this precise route.
The leprous men's distance can be compared with the law's separate dwelling for a person declared unclean. Leviticus does not name these ten men or independently establish their village or conduct.
Both healing petitions publicly invoke Jesus by name and ask mercy. The leprous group says Master; the blind beggar says Son of David. They are distinct recipients.
Both direct leprous recipients to show themselves to priests. Luke17 has ten cleansed while going; Luke5 concerns one already cleansed and additionally specifies Moses' offering.

Both cleansing accounts include a return and acknowledgment of God. Luke's healed man returns praising loudly; Naaman returns after Jordan washing and confesses Israel's God. The healers and occasions differ.

Both depict a cleansed recipient returning to the healer. Luke's Samaritan falls at Jesus' feet with thanks; Naaman stands before Elisha and acknowledges Israel's God. The persons and gestures differ.
Both connect healing with honoring God. Jesus notes the returning foreigner's gratitude; Naaman acknowledges no God except in Israel. Kings does not supply Luke's ten recipients or missing nine.
Both tell a healed recipient that faith has saved them and send them onward. Luke concerns a leprous man and says rise and go; Mark concerns bleeding and says go in peace.

Both address a question about kingdom timing without supplying the requested schedule. Luke answers Pharisees about observable coming; Acts answers disciples about the Father's appointed times. The questions and replies differ.

Both describe God's kingdom in relation to the present hearers. Luke17 says within you; Luke11 says has come upon you through God's exorcising work. The expressions are preserved without assigning them identical spatial meanings.
Both warn against pursuing localized claims about Christ or His presence. Matthew adds false messiahs, signs, wilderness and inner rooms; Luke simply rejects here-or-there reports.
Both compare the Son of Man's manifestation with widely visible lightning. Matthew specifies east and west; Luke describes one region under heaven shining to another.
Both predict the Son of Man's prior suffering and rejection. Luke names this generation; Mark specifies elders, chief priests and scribes, then death and resurrection.
Both compare Noah's days with the Son of Man's future manifestation. Matthew calls it His coming; Luke speaks of His days.
Both describe ordinary eating, drinking and marriage until Noah entered the ark and the flood swept people away. Matthew additionally emphasizes their lack of knowledge before the flood.

Both list ordinary activities before judgment. Luke adds Lot's setting, buying, selling, planting and building; Matthew names Noah's days and marriage. Matthew does not independently attest Luke's Lot-specific activity list.
Luke recalls Lot's departure followed by sulfur and fire destroying Sodom. Genesis places Lot in Zoar before the rain on Sodom and Gomorrah and describes the wider destruction.
Both apply an ancient sudden-destruction comparison to the Son of Man's future day. Luke follows Lot and says revealed; Matthew follows Noah and says coming.
Both forbid descending from a housetop for belongings or returning from a field. Matthew specifies taking a cloak; Luke's field instruction simply forbids turning back.
Jesus' command to remember Lot's wife points to Genesis' account of her looking back and becoming a salt pillar. Luke does not repeat those narrative details.
Both contrast saving life through losing it with losing life through trying to save it. Mark expressly names Jesus and the gospel as the reason; Luke's supplied saying omits that clause.
Both picture two people separated into taken and left. Luke places them on one bed at night; Matthew places them in a field. The settings are not merged.
Both describe two women grinding together, one taken and the other left. Neither verse names the women or specifies a separate destination.
Both connect a body or corpse with gathered eagles. Luke answers a Where question and says body; Matthew says corpse. Eagles is retained rather than replaced by another animal.
Both urge persistent prayer. Luke introduces a parable about praying always without losing heart; Thessalonians gives the brief command to pray without ceasing.
The widow's petition for justice corresponds to Isaiah's command to vindicate the widow and rescue the wronged. Isaiah gives a duty, not an independent report of this judge or case.
Both prayer illustrations include an initially unwilling respondent. Here an unjust judge delays; there a friend refuses a nighttime bread request. Their relationships and reasons differ.

Both reluctant respondents yield to insistent requests. The judge grants justice to avoid continual trouble; the friend supplies bread because of shameless insistence. Neither figure is simply identified with God.

Jesus directs attention to the unjust judge's stated reasoning: unwillingness gives way to the widow's persistence. This identifies the parable's quoted explanation rather than another judge or occasion.

Both associate persevering prayer with divine justice and deny that God simply delays it. Sirach describes humble prayer continuing until the Most High judges; Luke names chosen people crying day and night.
Both promise divine justice without delay. Sirach describes retribution and judgment for God's people; Luke promises speedy justice and adds the question of faith at the Son of Man's coming.

Both challenge self-justification before others. Luke18 introduces people trusting their own righteousness and despising others; Luke16 contrasts human self-justification with God's knowledge of hearts.

Both discuss meticulous tithing in religious self-presentation or criticism. Luke's speaker claims tithing everything and twice-weekly fasting; Matthew names herb tithes and neglected weightier duties, without that fasting schedule.
Both prayers address God for mercy in acknowledgment of sin. The tax collector calls himself the sinner; the psalm requests mercy and blotting out a lawless deed.
Both declare humiliation for self-exaltation and exaltation for self-humbling. Luke additionally gives the verdict that the tax collector, rather than the other man, went home justified.
Both describe children being brought for Jesus' touch and the disciples' rebukes. Luke explicitly includes infants; Mark uses children.
Both command allowing children to come without hindrance because God's kingdom belongs to such. Mark adds Jesus' indignation; Luke describes His calling them.
Both declare that receiving God's kingdom as a child is necessary for entering it.
Both record the Good Teacher question about inheriting eternal life. Luke identifies a ruler; Mark describes a man running and kneeling without that title.
Both question being called good and state that only God is good. No further identification or denial is added to the supplied words.
Both list commandments on adultery, murder, theft, false witness and honoring parents. The order differs, and Mark additionally includes do not defraud.
Both have the questioner claim observance of these commandments since youth. Mark additionally addresses Jesus as Teacher.
Both name one remaining lack and command sale, distribution to the poor and following Jesus, promising heavenly treasure. Mark additionally describes Jesus looking at and loving the man.
Both describe grief at the instruction because of great wealth. Mark also narrates departure; Luke's supplied verse does not say he left.
Both declare difficulty for wealthy people entering God's kingdom. Luke relates it to the man's grief; Mark describes Jesus looking around at His disciples.
Both compare a camel passing through a needle's eye with a rich person's entering God's kingdom. No alternative gate or altered animal is supplied.
Both report the hearers asking who can be saved. Mark describes heightened astonishment; Luke simply identifies those who heard.
Both contrast human impossibility with divine possibility. Mark explicitly says all things are possible with God; Luke says the things impossible with people are possible with God.
Both have Peter speak of leaving possessions or everything and following Jesus. Luke says what was our own; Mark says everything.
Both promise recompense for leaving household and family for Jesus' mission. Luke names wife and God's kingdom; Mark names fields and Jesus and the gospel. The lists remain distinct.
Both promise present recompense and eternal life in the coming age. Mark specifies a hundredfold, family and fields, and persecutions; Luke says many times as much without those additions.
Both describe the Jerusalem journey and taking the Twelve aside before a prediction. Luke expressly identifies fulfillment of prophetic writings; Mark does not repeat that formulation.
Both predict handing Jesus to the nations or Gentiles, mocking and spitting. Luke also says insulted; Mark names the preceding priestly condemnation and continues with flogging, death and rising.
Both predict flogging, killing and resurrection. Luke says on the third day; Mark says after three days. Those formulations are preserved.
Both state that disciples did not understand the saying and that it was hidden or veiled. Luke9 additionally describes their fear of asking, absent from this unit.

Both introduce a blind beggar at Jericho. Luke describes approaching the city; Mark describes departing and names Bartimaeus. No two-city explanation or identification of Luke's unnamed man is imposed.
Both identify the passing Jesus as the Nazarene. Luke reports others telling the beggar; Mark describes his hearing that identification before crying out.
Both give the blind beggar's appeal to Jesus, Son of David, for mercy. Mark introduces his cry after hearing Jesus was passing.
Both describe rebukes intended to silence the beggar and his louder repetition of the Son-of-David mercy appeal.
Both have Jesus stop and arrange the man's approach. Luke commands him to be brought; Mark commands a call and records the crowd's encouragement.
Both give Jesus' question about the desired action and the man's request for sight. Luke's address is Lord; Mark's is Rabbouni.
Both declare that faith has saved the man. Luke commands restored sight; Mark says go, followed by the narrated recovery.
Both narrate immediate sight and following Jesus. Luke adds the man's glorifying God and the people's praise, which Mark does not repeat.
Both place Jesus at Jericho. Luke narrates entry after the blind man's healing; Mark narrates arrival and departure before that healing. The differing sequences are not harmonized.

Luke introduces another wealthy encounter after the rich ruler's grief and Jesus' teaching on wealth, salvation and divine possibility. Zacchaeus's response and household salvation unfold in19:8-9. The named collector is not identified with the unnamed ruler, whose departure Luke does not narrate.
Both tax-collector scenes involve welcoming Jesus. Zacchaeus comes down rejoicing; Levi gives a great reception at home. The men and the details of their responses remain distinct.
Both describe grumbling over Jesus' hospitality with sinners. Here people object to lodging with Zacchaeus; Luke15 names Pharisees and scribes objecting to welcome and eating.

Both concern tax collectors and unjust gain. John forbids collecting beyond the prescribed amount; Zacchaeus says he gives half his goods to the poor and repays extortion fourfold. John does not prescribe those amounts.
Both affirm Abrahamic identity in connection with deliverance. Zacchaeus is called a son of Abraham as salvation reaches his house; the healed woman is Abraham's daughter released from Satan's bond.

Jesus' stated mission to seek and save the lost corresponds to the earlier lost-sheep search and its application to joy over repentance. Zacchaeus is not assigned an exclusive identity as the parable's sheep.

Both address expectations about the kingdom's arrival. Luke19 explains an expectation of immediate appearance near Jerusalem; Luke17 records Pharisees' timing question and Jesus' reply about observable coming. The audiences and answers differ.
Both introduce an absent master before entrusted servants' activity. Luke's nobleman travels to receive a kingdom and return; Matthew's traveler entrusts possessions without that royal mission.

Both entrust money to slaves before departure. Luke gives ten minas to ten slaves with a business command; Matthew distributes five, two and one talents according to ability. No currency conversion or identical allocation is inferred.

The later command against enemies who refused his reign recalls the citizens' rejecting delegation. The command is not a narration of an execution already carried out, and citizens are not automatically equated with the entrusted slaves.
Both describe a returned master calling entrusted servants to account. Luke expressly says he received the kingdom and asks about business; Matthew specifies a long absence before settling accounts.
Both servants report profitable use of entrusted money. Luke's mina gains ten minas; Matthew's five talents gain five more. The currencies, initial amounts and ratios differ.
Both praise a good servant's faithfulness in little and grant greater responsibility. Luke specifies ten cities; Matthew promises appointment over many things and entry into the master's joy.
Both second servants report gain. Luke reports one mina making five; Matthew reports two talents gaining two more. These are not identical investments or returns.
Both reward the second profitable servant with responsibility. Luke grants five cities; Matthew repeats praise and appointment over many things, with the master's joy.
Both servants return money kept unused. Luke's mina was laid away in a cloth; Matthew's talent was hidden in the ground, with fear stated in that verse.

Both fearful servants describe the master as reaping without sowing. Luke says severe and taking what was not laid down; Matthew says hard and gathering where not scattered. These remain the servants' descriptions.

Both masters answer the servant through his own depiction of their severity. Luke explicitly judges from his mouth and calls him evil; Matthew calls him evil and idle. The accusation is not independently verified as the master's character.
Both ask why money was not deposited so it could be received with interest on return. The comparison concerns the parables' rebukes, not a separate financial recommendation.
Both order the unused money taken and given to the servant with ten. Luke names a mina and ten minas; Matthew names a talent and ten talents. The units are preserved.
Both state that one who has receives more while one who lacks loses even what he has. Matthew adds abundance; Luke introduces the saying with I tell you.

The command concerning enemies who rejected the king's reign explicitly recalls the earlier delegation's refusal. The text reports the story character's command rather than narrating its execution, and does not identify every entrusted slave with the rejecting citizens.

Both describe Jesus going ahead on the ascent toward Jerusalem. Mark additionally describes followers' amazement and fear and introduces a prediction; Luke places this movement after the mina parable.
Both locate the approach near Bethphage, Bethany and the Mount of Olives and describe sending two disciples. Luke calls the mount Olivet; Mark names it in its own supplied form.
Both direct the disciples to a nearby village, where an unridden colt is tied, and command its untying and bringing. Luke says on entering; Mark says immediately on entering.
Both prescribe answering a challenge by saying the Lord needs the colt. Mark additionally mentions sending it back immediately; Luke's supplied instruction does not.
Both narrate the disciples finding the colt after Jesus' instruction. Luke says just as told; Mark specifies a door outside on the street and begins the untying.
Both describe an objection while the colt is untied. Luke identifies the questioners as its owners; Mark calls them people standing there.
Both describe answering as Jesus instructed. Luke repeats the Lord's need; Mark summarizes the instructed answer and says the bystanders let them go.
Both bring the colt to Jesus and put garments on it for Him. Luke says they set Jesus on it; Mark says He sat on it.
Both describe garments spread on the road. Mark additionally mentions leafy branches cut from fields; Luke does not supply them here.

Both describe acclaim during Jesus' approach. Luke specifies disciples descending the mount and praising for seen mighty works; Mark describes those ahead and behind acclaiming the coming one and Davidic kingdom.

Luke's blessing of the King coming in the Lord's name recalls the psalm's blessing of the one coming in His name. Luke adds King, heavenly peace and highest glory; the psalm continues with blessing from the Lord's house.
Both acclamations join peace with glory in the highest. The infancy angels say peace on earth; the entering disciples say peace in heaven. The speakers and locations of peace are distinguished.

Both describe objections to praise of Jesus. Luke names Pharisees demanding rebuke of disciples during the approach; Matthew names priests and scribes reacting to children's temple cries. The groups, settings and replies differ.

Both personify a stone crying out. Habakkuk's wall-stone witnesses within a woe against unjust gain; Jesus says stones will cry if disciples fall silent. Their occasions and purposes are not identified.

Both portray Jesus grieving over Jerusalem. Luke narrates His weeping at the city's sight; Matthew gives His lament over rejected gathering and killed prophets without independently reporting these tears.

Both lament missed peace associated with failure to heed. Isaiah pictures peace like a river if commands had been heard; Jesus speaks of the city's failure to know peace now hidden. The occasions and imagery differ.

Both describe a city surrounded by siege works. Isaiah's divine speaker promises encirclement, a palisade and towers; Luke names enemies hemming the city in with a siege barrier. The speakers and exact details differ.
Both predict that stone will not remain upon stone. Luke19 concerns the city, its children and missed visitation; Luke21 addresses the temple buildings. The scopes are not silently equated.
Both narrate Jesus driving sellers from the temple. Mark also mentions buyers, money-changers' tables and dove-sellers' seats; Luke's present unit does not.
Both call God's house a house of prayer. Isaiah adds for all nations and describes offerings; Luke's supplied citation does not repeat that phrase or the entire verse.
Jesus' den-of-robbers rebuke recalls Jeremiah's question about the house called by God's name becoming a robbers' cave. Jeremiah supplies the temple critique, not an account of this later expulsion.
Both describe chief priests and scribes seeking to destroy Jesus in the temple-teaching context. Luke adds daily teaching and leading men; Mark explains the leaders' fear and the crowd's amazement.
Both connect the leaders' difficulty acting with the crowd's response to Jesus' teaching. Luke says people hung on His words; Mark says the crowd was astonished, causing the leaders' fear.
Both introduce chief priests, scribes and elders approaching Jesus in the temple. Luke describes teaching and good-news proclamation; Mark describes His walking there.
Both question Jesus' authority and who gave it to Him. Neither verse itself defines the challengers' demanded authorization.
Both answer the authority challenge with Jesus proposing a question. Mark explicitly says their answer will precede His explanation; Luke's shorter introduction continues into the baptism question.
Both ask whether John's baptism came from heaven or from people. Mark adds answer Me.
Both give the leaders' reasoning that admitting heavenly origin invites Jesus' question why they did not believe John.
Both fear the public response to denying John's prophetic status. Luke expressly predicts stoning; Mark describes fear of the crowd because all considered John truly a prophet.
Both report the leaders answering that they do not know. Luke explicitly names uncertainty about the baptism's source; Mark also gives Jesus' ensuing refusal.
Both have Jesus refuse to disclose His authority after their nonanswer. Mark combines their answer and His refusal in one unit.
Both introduce a planted vineyard leased to farmers during the owner's absence. Mark adds fence, winepress and tower; Luke specifies a considerable time away.
Both describe a seasonal servant sent for vineyard produce, beaten and sent away empty. Mark divides the sending and mistreatment across two units.
Both describe a second servant being beaten and dishonored. Mark specifies a head injury; Luke additionally says he was sent away empty. The injuries are not made identical.
Both describe another servant sent and mistreated. Luke's third is wounded and thrown out; Mark says the next was killed and adds many others beaten or killed. The severity and sequence differ.
Both turn to sending a beloved son with an expectation of respect. Luke says perhaps; Mark states they will respect him and calls him the last sending.
Both have the farmers identify the heir and propose killing him to obtain the inheritance.
Both narrate the son's killing and expulsion and ask what the owner will do. Luke puts expulsion before killing; Mark puts killing before expulsion. The action order is preserved.
Both answer that the owner destroys the farmers and gives the vineyard to others. Luke additionally records the hearers' May it never happen response.
Both identify the builders' rejected stone as the head of the corner. Luke introduces the written saying as a question to the hearers; the psalm does not narrate their parable.

Both describe a person falling on the stone being shattered and a person under the falling stone being crushed. The saying is retained without assigning an extra physical location or historical victim.
Both describe leaders seeking to seize Jesus, fearing the crowd and recognizing the vineyard parable against them. Mark adds their departure; Luke specifies that very hour.
Both describe agents sent to trap Jesus in speech. Luke calls them spies feigning righteousness and names handing Him to the governor as the aim; Mark names Pharisees and Herodians.
Both preface the tax question by calling Jesus a truthful, impartial teacher of God's way. Mark also includes the tax question in the same unit.
Both ask whether paying Caesar's tribute is lawful. Mark adds whether they should pay and Jesus' recognition and request for a denarius; Luke places those developments in following units.
Both have Jesus recognize the questioners' duplicity. Luke says cunning; Mark says hypocrisy and quotes His challenge about testing and His coin request.
Both ask whose image and inscription the denarius bears and receive Caesar as the answer. Luke includes Jesus' request to show the coin; Mark narrates its production.
Both command rendering Caesar's things to Caesar and God's things to God. Mark also reports the hearers' amazement in that unit.
Both describe amazement at Jesus' answer. Luke additionally states they could not seize His words before the people and fell silent; Mark does not repeat those details.
Both introduce Sadducees who deny resurrection approaching with a question. The denial is theirs, not the narrator's endorsement.

The cited Mosaic rule corresponds to a dead childless brother's widow being taken by his brother to continue the dead man's line. Deuteronomy adds co-residing brothers and establishing the child's name for the dead; Luke summarizes the rule in the challengers' question.
Both begin the hypothetical case with seven brothers and the first marrying and dying without offspring.

Luke's short continuation names the second brother; Mark explicitly narrates his marriage and childless death before the third. Luke's saved fragment is read with its surrounding units, not expanded in the source.
Both continue through the third and the seven brothers, all without offspring. Mark also states the woman's final death, which Luke gives in the following unit.
Both conclude the hypothetical sequence with the woman's death after the brothers. Mark combines it with the seven leaving no offspring.
Both ask whose wife the woman will be in the resurrection because all seven married her.

Jesus' statement about present-age marriage is explicitly contrasted with the next unit's resurrection-age absence of marriage. This preserves the distinction between ages rather than applying the later condition indiscriminately to present life.
Both say those raised neither marry nor are given in marriage. Luke names the coming age and those counted worthy; Mark proceeds to the angel comparison.

Both compare resurrection life with angels. Luke adds inability to die and divine sonship through resurrection; Mark says like angels in the heavens. Luke's additional claims are not inserted into Mark.

Jesus invokes the bush passage's identification of God with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Exodus gives that divine self-identification; Luke uses it in a resurrection argument not stated in full within Exodus.
Both call God the God of living rather than dead people. Luke adds that all live to Him; Mark concludes that the questioners are greatly mistaken.

Both have scribes commend Jesus as Teacher for speaking well. Luke has several respond after the resurrection discussion; Mark has one respond after the love-command discussion. Their occasions and statements are not merged.
Both conclude that people no longer dared question Jesus. Luke follows the resurrection exchange; Mark follows the love-command discussion. The differing sequence is preserved.
Both ask how the Christ can be called David's son. Mark explicitly attributes that description to scribes while Jesus teaches in the temple.
Luke quotes the psalm's Lord-to-my-lord speech and invitation to sit at God's right hand. The same psalm verse continues with the enemies' footstool clause quoted in Luke's next unit.

Luke's enemies-as-footstool clause continues the same psalm verse quoted immediately before. The target retains its Davidic heading and complete speech rather than being renumbered to another Psalter.
Both ask how David's calling the Christ Lord relates to calling Him David's son. Mark additionally describes the crowd's glad hearing; no extra genealogical or chronological conclusion is imposed.

Both place a public teaching warning about scribes after the David discussion. Luke distinguishes listening people from addressed disciples; Mark mentions the crowd's glad hearing and introduces the warning without that same audience distinction.
Both warn about scribes' robes, marketplace greetings, foremost synagogue seats and foremost places at meals. Mark distributes the list across two units.
Both condemn devouring widows' houses and lengthy prayers as pretext, followed by greater judgment. Their supplied formulations agree on the warning; no different victim group is inferred.

deferred.reason: Jesus' question about ten cleansed and nine absent is distinctive to this healing account. Other healing or gratitude scenes do not establish these numbers or the absent recipients' actions.
The predicted longing for one of the Son of Man's days without seeing it has no sufficiently precise retained counterpart. Other wishes to see Jesus are not treated as this same future experience.
The judge's particular lack of fear of God and respect for people is distinctive characterization. Other unjust officials are not equated with this parable figure.
The paired temple visit of a Pharisee and tax collector is this parable's specific setup. Other temple prayers do not independently establish these two figures or their visit.

The Pharisee's comparative thanksgiving and its particular list of other people's vices have no sufficiently precise retained counterpart. General pride sayings do not independently reproduce this prayer.
The blind man's question about the passing crowd is a distinctive transition. Another account's report that he heard about Jesus does not independently reproduce this particular question.
Zacchaeus's short stature and inability to see through the crowd are distinctive personal details. Other crowd impediments do not establish his circumstances.
Running ahead and climbing a sycamore fig tree to see Jesus are distinctive details. Unrelated tree or climbing passages do not supply a defensible counterpart.
Jesus' personal summons from the tree and statement that He must stay in Zacchaeus's house today are distinctive. Other calls and hospitality scenes do not independently reproduce this directive.
The bystanders' objection that the recipient already has ten minas is distinctive to this parable. The talent story does not include that interjection, and it was not silently supplied there.

review_notes: All174 actual original source units were read in order:Luke17 has36, Luke18 has43, Luke19 has48, Luke20 has47. Luke17:36 is absent in the pinned original and is not invented or counted. Every retained target was read with surrounding context.

164 distinct source units have166 retained pairs;10 units are deferred with zero completion credit. Extra targets explain the scriptural and same-book praise language at19:38 and the two scriptural clauses at19:46.

Original source wording, display text, numbering gaps and continuation fragments are unchanged. Luke20:30 remains its actual brief continuation. Original target ranges retain full contiguous saved units, including the complete Psalm headings and Matthew25:15's trailing continuation word.

Same-book comparisons are labeled as teaching, journey, contrast, interpretation, narrative callback or hospitality links rather than independent witnesses. The slave-service examples preserve reversed roles; internal duty applications and repeated refusal-of-rule language remain explicit.

Sirach35 uses this edition's actual divisions and wording for persistent humble prayer and divine justice. No universal calendar or blanket identity between reluctant human respondents and God is inferred.

The rich ruler, Zacchaeus and other tax collectors are distinguished. Zacchaeus's statement about giving and fourfold repayment is retained as a statement without deciding whether it describes an existing practice or a new resolution. No inherited wealth, legal fourfold requirement or other collector's identity is supplied.

Luke's approach to Jericho and Mark's departure notice are preserved without a two-Jericho theory, forced sequence or naming Luke's unnamed beggar as Bartimaeus. Faith and healing pronouncements retain their different recipients and added phrases.

The mina/talent comparisons preserve ten slaves versus differently allocated talents, money units, returns, cities, cloth versus ground, citizens versus servants, and stated accusations versus independently established facts. The king's execution command is not narrated as already carried out.

Entry acclamations distinguish disciples from children, Pharisees from priests and scribes, peace in heaven from infancy peace on earth, and Psalm117's wording from Luke's additions. Habakkuk's crying stone remains a bounded imagery comparison.

Jerusalem's city-level siege and visitation language is distinguished from the temple-building prediction. Isaiah29's palisade and towers, Isaiah48's missed peace and actual Psalm109/117 numbering are retained.

Vineyard mistreatment keeps wounded versus killed servants and the differing order of the son's expulsion and killing. Debate agents, tax-question motives, no-more-questioning sequence, and scriptural marriage and resurrection arguments remain distinct.

Deuteronomy25:6 is read as this original supplies it:the child is established in the dead man's name; an imported firstborn qualification is not added. Angel comparisons do not silently import Luke's immortality and sonship language into Mark.
ID existence, original-order target contiguity, unique directed pairs, no self-targets and complete source coverage were verified. No John source review was begun.
